en.greeting: Hi! Today you listen for what people mean but don't say: understatement, irony, reluctance and polite refusals. Then you follow messy, unplanned talk in interviews and panels, and take lecture notes that keep what matters. Play each recording as often as you like.

steps.title: Words vs. facts
steps.text: You already separate facts from opinions and know the real opinion comes after **however** or **that said**. Now the opinion is often not said at all: it's **implied** (hidden in how something is said).
steps.body: **Understatement:** soft words for a big problem. *not exactly* + a positive word = the opposite: *It wasn't exactly a success* = it failed. *I've had better days* = a bad day. *a bit of a problem* = a serious one. **Faint praise:** asked about something important, the speaker praises only something small: about his work, *Well, he's always on time* = his work isn't good. The method: compare the **words** with the **facts** around them; when they don't match, believe the facts. British *not bad* often means quite good.

pairs.id: Pernah lebih baik. → hari ini buruk
Yah, dia selalu tepat waktu. → (tentang kerjanya) tidak ada yang bisa dipuji

steps.title: Listen: a founder looks back
steps.text: This is from a podcast interview with the founder of a Jakarta startup. Compare the words with the facts.

question.listen: Our first year? Well, it wasn't exactly the dream start we'd hoped for. We spent most of our money on an office we hardly used, our first app had, let's say, a few problems, and two of my co-founders left. But we learnt a lot.
question.prompt: The host asks about the company's first year. Listen to the founder's answer. How did the first year really go?
options: It went very badly.
It went well, with a few small problems.
It was the dream start the founders wanted.
question.explanation: **wasn't exactly the dream start** is understatement: *not exactly* + a positive phrase = the opposite. The facts confirm it: most of the money was wasted, the app had problems (*let's say, a few* softens it) and two co-founders left. 'A few small problems' takes the soft words literally.

steps.title: Irony, reluctance and a polite no
steps.text: Three more patterns. Again, the words tell you; in real life tone helps too, but our audio is one calm voice.
steps.body: **Irony:** positive words + a clearly bad situation = the opposite. *Oh great, another meeting about meetings* = annoyed. **Reluctance:** yes, but unwillingly: *I suppose I could, if no one else is free*, *If I have to*, *Fine, I'll do it*. **Hedged refusal:** a polite no: *That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it*, *I'll see what I can do*, *Maybe next year*. Indonesian has the same habits (*nanti saya pikir-pikir dulu*, *lihat nanti ya*). The trap is to think English speakers always say exactly what they mean.

pairs.en: Oh great. Just what I needed.
It wouldn't be my first choice.

pairs.id: Aku pikir-pikir dulu. → sering berarti tidak

pairs.en: I'll see what I can do.
pairs.id: Nanti aku lihat bisa atau tidak. → kemungkinan tidak

steps.title: Listen: a new idea from staff
steps.text: This is from an online panel about remote work. The host asks Bu Wulan, an HR director, about an idea from her staff.

question.listen: Letting staff work from Bali for a month? That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it. Of course, I'd need to talk to the board first, and to IT, and to our clients. So, maybe next year. Or the year after.
question.prompt: Listen to Bu Wulan's answer. What does she really mean?
options: She likes the idea and will try it soon.
She has already discussed it with the board.
She's politely saying that it probably won't happen.
question.explanation: **That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it** is a hedged refusal: a polite no. The long list of people to ask and **maybe next year. Or the year after** push the idea far away. She says she would *need to* talk to the board, so she hasn't done it yet.

steps.title: Messy talk: interviews and panels
steps.text: Interviews and panels aren't planned like lectures. Few signposts, lots of changes.
steps.body: Track four things. **Who holds which view:** *I'm with Sari on that* = I agree with Sari; *I'd push back on what Dimas said* = I disagree. Keep a list: NAME = VIEW. Careful: speakers often repeat a view in order to reject it. **Topic shifts:** *Anyway…*, *Oh, and…*, *Going back to…*. **Self-corrections:** after *sorry*, *I mean*, *or rather*, *well*, **the last version is the fact**: *about fifty, sorry, fifteen* = 15. **Asides:** *by the way*, *not that it matters*, *where was I?*: not the main point. Ignore fillers: *you know*, *sort of*.

pairs.id: …, atau lebih tepatnya, … → versi baru = fakta
Pokoknya / omong-omong… → ganti atau kembali ke topik
Tadi sampai mana? → kembali ke poin utama

steps.title: Listen: plans that change
steps.text: Back to the startup podcast. The founder talks about new cities. Listen to the end of each sentence before you decide.

question.listen: We're opening in Surabaya in May, well, June, realistically, because the licence always takes longer than you think. Makassar was on the plan for this year too, but honestly, that's next year now. Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, Surabaya first.
question.prompt: Listen to the founder. When will the company open in Surabaya?
options: In May
In June
Next year
question.explanation: **May, well, June, realistically** is a self-correction: the last version, **June**, is the fact. *Next year* is about Makassar, not Surabaya. **Anyway, where was I?** brings the speaker back to the main topic: Surabaya.

steps.title: Listen: who thinks what?
steps.text: This is one panellist's turn in the online panel on remote work. Two other panellists, Dimas and Sari, spoke earlier.

question.listen: I'd push back a little on what Dimas said. He thinks new graduates learn best at home, with online training. In my experience, they learn by sitting next to someone experienced. Sari's point about saving travel time is fair, though. I'm with her on that.
question.prompt: Listen to the panellist. Which sentence matches the panellist's views?
options: The panellist agrees with Dimas about online training.
The panellist disagrees with both Dimas and Sari.
The panellist disagrees with Dimas, but agrees with Sari about travel time.
question.explanation: **I'd push back a little on what Dimas said** = I disagree with Dimas. The online-training view is Dimas's, repeated so the panellist can reject it. **Sari's point … is fair, though. I'm with her on that** = I agree with Sari.

steps.title: Lecture notes: keep what matters
steps.text: Last skill: notes in a long lecture. You can't write everything, and you shouldn't.
steps.body: Listen for **'this is important' signals** and mark the note (**!!**, **NB**, *exam*): *The key point here is…*, *Let me stress…*, *This will come up again*, *Make a note of this*. Write numbers and names at once; after a correction, keep only the final version. **Skip** examples you already know, repetition (*In other words…*), jokes and asides. Use symbols: **↑ ↓ →**, and new: **∴** therefore, **≈** about, **vs** compared with. **Cornell** page: key words on the left, notes on the right, a 1–2 sentence summary at the bottom.

pairs.id: Ini akan muncul lagi. → tandai: exam

pairs.en: You all know…, so I'll skip that.
pairs.id: Kalian semua tahu…, jadi saya lewati. → jangan dicatat

steps.title: Listen: the best note
steps.text: This is part of a lecture on urban transport at a university in Yogyakarta. Imagine your notes: what do you keep, what do you skip?

question.listen: Right, you all know Jalan Malioboro, so I won't describe it again. Let me stress this, because it'll come up again: when cities widen their roads, traffic doesn't go down. It goes up, because wider roads attract more cars. This is called induced demand.
question.prompt: Listen to the lecture extract. Which note is the most useful?
options: Malioboro: busy, famous street
wider roads → more cars ∴ traffic ↑ (induced demand) !! exam
wider roads → traffic ↓ (induced demand)
question.explanation: **Let me stress this, because it'll come up again** marks the key point: wider roads attract more cars, so traffic goes **up** (↑), not down. Malioboro is an example you already know: the lecturer even says so. The third note misses the **doesn't** in *traffic doesn't go down*.

steps.title: Quick review
steps.text: Flip each card. Try to say the English before you look.

flashcards.back: Oh great. Just what I needed.
I suppose I could, if no one else is free.
That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it.

flashcards.front: Koreksi diri: mana faktanya? 'May, well, June'
flashcards.back: June: the last version is the fact.
Let me stress… / This will come up again.

steps.title: Listen more
steps.text: Two C1 recordings with transcripts: an interview with three voices and implied opinions, and a lecture to practise Cornell notes.

id.greeting: Hai! Hari ini kamu menyimak hal yang dimaksud orang tapi tidak diucapkan: understatement, ironi, keengganan dan penolakan halus. Lalu kamu mengikuti obrolan yang tidak rapi di wawancara dan panel, dan membuat catatan kuliah yang menyimpan hal penting. Putar setiap rekaman sesering yang kamu mau.

steps.title: Kata-kata vs. fakta
steps.text: Kamu sudah bisa memisahkan fakta dari opini dan tahu bahwa opini sebenarnya datang setelah **however** atau **that said**. Sekarang opininya sering tidak diucapkan sama sekali: opininya **tersirat** (implied).
steps.body: **Understatement** (mengecilkan): kata halus untuk masalah besar. *not exactly* + kata positif = kebalikannya: *It wasn't exactly a success* = gagal. *I've had better days* = hari yang buruk. *a bit of a problem* = masalah serius. **Pujian tipis** (faint praise): ditanya hal yang penting, pembicara hanya memuji hal kecil: tentang kerjanya, *Well, he's always on time* = kerjanya kurang bagus. Caranya: bandingkan **kata-katanya** dengan **fakta** di sekitarnya; kalau tidak cocok, percayai faktanya. *Not bad* gaya British sering berarti cukup bagus.

pairs.id: Pernah lebih baik. → hari ini buruk
Yah, dia selalu tepat waktu. → (tentang kerjanya) tidak ada yang bisa dipuji

steps.title: Dengarkan: pendiri startup menengok ke belakang
steps.text: Ini dari wawancara podcast dengan pendiri sebuah startup di Jakarta. Bandingkan kata-katanya dengan faktanya.

question.listen: Our first year? Well, it wasn't exactly the dream start we'd hoped for. We spent most of our money on an office we hardly used, our first app had, let's say, a few problems, and two of my co-founders left. But we learnt a lot.
question.prompt: Pembawa acara bertanya tentang tahun pertama perusahaannya. Dengarkan jawaban si pendiri. Sebenarnya bagaimana tahun pertamanya?
options: It went very badly.
It went well, with a few small problems.
It was the dream start the founders wanted.
question.explanation: **wasn't exactly the dream start** (bukan awal impian juga sih) adalah understatement: *not exactly* + frasa positif = kebalikannya. Faktanya membuktikan: sebagian besar uang terbuang, aplikasinya bermasalah (*let's say, a few* melunakkannya) dan dua co-founder keluar. 'A few small problems' menelan kata-kata halusnya mentah-mentah.
displayOptions: Berjalan baik, dengan beberapa masalah kecil.

steps.title: Ironi, keengganan dan 'tidak' yang sopan
steps.text: Tiga pola lagi. Sekali lagi, kata-katanya yang memberitahumu; di dunia nyata nada suara juga membantu, tapi audio kita satu suara yang tenang.
steps.body: **Ironi:** kata positif + situasi yang jelas buruk = kebalikannya. *Oh great, another meeting about meetings* = kesal. **Keengganan:** mau, tapi terpaksa: *I suppose I could, if no one else is free*, *If I have to*, *Fine, I'll do it*. **Penolakan halus:** 'tidak' yang sopan: *That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it*, *I'll see what I can do*, *Maybe next year*. Bahasa Indonesia punya kebiasaan yang sama (*nanti saya pikir-pikir dulu*, *lihat nanti ya*). Jebakannya: mengira penutur bahasa Inggris selalu bicara apa adanya.

pairs.en: Oh great. Just what I needed.
It wouldn't be my first choice.

pairs.id: Aku pikir-pikir dulu. → sering berarti tidak

pairs.en: I'll see what I can do.
pairs.id: Nanti aku lihat bisa atau tidak. → kemungkinan tidak

steps.title: Dengarkan: ide baru dari karyawan
steps.text: Ini dari panel online tentang kerja jarak jauh. Pembawa acara bertanya kepada Bu Wulan, direktur HR, tentang ide dari karyawannya.

question.listen: Letting staff work from Bali for a month? That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it. Of course, I'd need to talk to the board first, and to IT, and to our clients. So, maybe next year. Or the year after.
question.prompt: Dengarkan jawaban Bu Wulan. Apa maksudnya yang sebenarnya?
options: She likes the idea and will try it soon.
She has already discussed it with the board.
She's politely saying that it probably won't happen.
question.explanation: **That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it** adalah penolakan halus: 'tidak' yang sopan. Daftar panjang orang yang harus ditanya dan **maybe next year. Or the year after** (mungkin tahun depan, atau tahun depannya lagi) mendorong idenya jauh-jauh. Ia bilang ia *perlu* bicara dengan direksi, jadi ia belum melakukannya.
displayOptions: Dia menyukai idenya dan akan segera mencobanya.
Dia mengatakan dengan sopan bahwa hal itu mungkin tidak akan terwujud.

steps.title: Obrolan tidak rapi: wawancara dan panel
steps.text: Wawancara dan panel tidak direncanakan seperti kuliah. Sedikit penanda, banyak perubahan.
steps.body: Ikuti empat hal. **Siapa berpendapat apa:** *I'm with Sari on that* = saya setuju dengan Sari; *I'd push back on what Dimas said* = saya kurang setuju. Buat daftar: NAMA = PENDAPAT. Hati-hati: pembicara sering mengulang pendapat orang lain untuk menolaknya. **Pindah topik:** *Anyway…*, *Oh, and…*, *Going back to…*. **Koreksi diri:** setelah *sorry*, *I mean*, *or rather*, *well*, **versi terakhir = fakta**: *about fifty, sorry, fifteen* = 15. **Selingan:** *by the way*, *not that it matters*, *where was I?*: bukan poin utama. Abaikan kata pengisi: *you know*, *sort of*.

pairs.id: …, atau lebih tepatnya, … → versi baru = fakta
Pokoknya / omong-omong… → ganti atau kembali ke topik
Tadi sampai mana? → kembali ke poin utama

steps.title: Dengarkan: rencana yang berubah
steps.text: Kembali ke podcast startup tadi. Si pendiri bicara tentang kota-kota baru. Dengarkan sampai akhir kalimat sebelum memutuskan.

question.listen: We're opening in Surabaya in May, well, June, realistically, because the licence always takes longer than you think. Makassar was on the plan for this year too, but honestly, that's next year now. Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, Surabaya first.
question.prompt: Dengarkan si pendiri. Kapan perusahaannya buka di Surabaya?
options: In May
In June
Next year
question.explanation: **May, well, June, realistically** (Mei, eh, Juni kalau realistis) adalah koreksi diri: versi terakhirnya, **June**, itulah faktanya. *Next year* tentang Makassar, bukan Surabaya. **Anyway, where was I?** (omong-omong, tadi sampai mana?) membawa pembicara kembali ke topik utama: Surabaya.

steps.title: Dengarkan: siapa berpendapat apa?
steps.text: Ini giliran bicara seorang panelis di panel online tentang kerja jarak jauh. Dua panelis lain, Dimas dan Sari, sudah bicara sebelumnya.

question.listen: I'd push back a little on what Dimas said. He thinks new graduates learn best at home, with online training. In my experience, they learn by sitting next to someone experienced. Sari's point about saving travel time is fair, though. I'm with her on that.
question.prompt: Dengarkan panelis itu. Kalimat mana yang cocok dengan pendapat panelis tersebut?
options: The panellist agrees with Dimas about online training.
The panellist disagrees with both Dimas and Sari.
The panellist disagrees with Dimas, but agrees with Sari about travel time.
question.explanation: **I'd push back a little on what Dimas said** = saya agak kurang setuju dengan Dimas. Pendapat soal pelatihan online itu milik Dimas, diulang supaya panelis bisa menolaknya. **Sari's point … is fair, though. I'm with her on that** = poin Sari masuk akal; saya setuju dengannya.
displayOptions: Panelis setuju dengan Dimas tentang pelatihan online.
Panelis tidak setuju dengan Dimas maupun Sari.
Panelis tidak setuju dengan Dimas, tetapi setuju dengan Sari tentang waktu perjalanan.

steps.title: Catatan kuliah: simpan yang penting
steps.text: Keterampilan terakhir: mencatat kuliah yang panjang. Kamu tidak bisa mencatat semuanya, dan memang tidak perlu.
steps.body: Dengarkan **sinyal 'ini penting'** lalu tandai catatannya (**!!**, **NB**, *exam*): *The key point here is…*, *Let me stress…*, *This will come up again*, *Make a note of this*. Tulis angka dan nama saat itu juga; setelah ada koreksi, simpan versi terakhirnya saja. **Lewati** contoh yang sudah kamu tahu, pengulangan (*In other words…*), lelucon dan selingan. Pakai simbol: **↑ ↓ →**, dan yang baru: **∴** maka, **≈** kira-kira, **vs** dibandingkan dengan. Halaman **Cornell**: kata kunci di kiri, catatan di kanan, ringkasan 1–2 kalimat di bawah.

pairs.en: You all know…, so I'll skip that.
pairs.id: Kalian semua tahu…, jadi saya lewati. → jangan dicatat

steps.title: Dengarkan: catatan terbaik
steps.text: Ini bagian dari kuliah tentang transportasi kota di sebuah universitas di Yogyakarta. Bayangkan catatanmu: apa yang disimpan, apa yang dilewati?

question.listen: Right, you all know Jalan Malioboro, so I won't describe it again. Let me stress this, because it'll come up again: when cities widen their roads, traffic doesn't go down. It goes up, because wider roads attract more cars. This is called induced demand.
question.prompt: Dengarkan cuplikan kuliahnya. Catatan mana yang paling berguna?
options: Malioboro: busy, famous street
wider roads → more cars ∴ traffic ↑ (induced demand) !! exam
wider roads → traffic ↓ (induced demand)
question.explanation: **Let me stress this, because it'll come up again** (saya tekankan ini, karena akan muncul lagi) menandai poin kuncinya: jalan yang lebih lebar menarik lebih banyak mobil, jadi kemacetan **naik** (↑), bukan turun. Malioboro adalah contoh yang sudah kamu kenal: dosennya sendiri bilang begitu. Catatan ketiga melewatkan kata **doesn't** di *traffic doesn't go down*.
